Chapter 5: Delete Characters

This chapter adds delete behavior without moving collection ownership, delete rules, or confirmation logic into the template. The workflow now supports destructive updates through the same service-owned boundary.

Keep the same split in place: the service is still the only place that updates committed Feature State, while the component owns local selection, confirmation, editor, and feedback state. Keeping that line clear makes delete behavior easier to follow and easier to maintain.

Make destructive changes explicit, confirmable, and state-safe.

Deletion changes more than a button label: it removes a record from the feature's committed collection and can be difficult to undo. This chapter adds a deliberate confirmation point while keeping the actual removal on the same service-owned pipeline used for every other mutation.

Why this boundary matters

The component coordinates selection, confirmation, and feedback, but it never edits the committed collection directly. The service owns the destructive policy and submits the target identity through mergeState() with isDelete: true. Array By ID Merge applies the identifier-based removal while keeping the operation consistent with the rest of the Feature State lifecycle.

Use this structure for

  • removing a saved item after an explicit confirmation
  • revoking an assignment or removing access to a record
  • deleting a draft while preserving a clear cancellation path

By the end of this chapter

You will have a pending-delete state, a cancelable confirmation flow, and a service-owned removal method that removes the selected character by identity while preserving every other committed record.

Chapter 5 Starting Point and Change Map

Start with the completed Chapter 4 project. Add one service removal method, then add component-local pending-delete state, request/cancel/confirm handlers, confirmation markup, and focused tests. Register Array By ID Merge for the FeatureCell, then use mergeState() for create and update operations. Deletion submits the target identity with isDelete: true so the active behavior removes the matching record.

What “Destructive” Means Here

The array transformation is immutable, but the user-visible record is intentionally removed from committed State. This browser-only tutorial does not implement server authorization, durable deletion, undo, optimistic rollback, or audit logging. Add those controls at the real persistence boundary in production.

Step 1: Configure Array By Id Merge Behavior
↑ top

Before the service can delete a character correctly, the registered needs identifier-based array merge semantics. In the previous chapter, it used append-style merge semantics for adding new characters.

Now we need to switch to Array By ID Merge so matching records can be updated, new records can be appended, and delete requests can remove records by identifier.

To change that Merge-stage behavior, install the package and register withArrayByIdMergeBehavior in app.config.ts. This makes mergeState() compare records by their identifier during the Merge stage.

Make the Change
  1. Install the package. 
    npm install @sdux-vault/addons
  2. Open app.config.ts
  3. Import withArrayByIdMergeBehavior from .
  4. Pass [withArrayByIdMergeBehavior] as the behavior list for provide(). 
    {{ appConfigFile().source }}
Why This Behavior Is Required
  • mergeState() submits the incoming records and merge configuration to the active Array By ID Merge behavior.
  • The behavior updates an existing record when its identifier matches and appends incoming records with new identifiers.
  • With withArrayByIdMergeBehavior, setting isDelete on a merge request removes the matching record from the collection.
  • This keeps identifier matching and collection changes in the Merge stage instead of requiring the service to manually find, replace, append, or remove records.
Avoid Manual Array Merging

You could build the next collection manually with a spread expression such as [...currentCharacters, newCharacter], but that only covers appending. It does not provide the identifier-based update and deletion rules required by this tutorial.

The spread operator itself does not mutate the array. The anti-pattern is pushing identifier-based merge policy into the service instead of configuring it in the pipeline. Register Array By ID Merge for the FeatureCell, then let mergeState() apply matching, appending, and isDelete rules consistently.

Step 2: Add the Delete Service Slice
↑ top

This is the point where the tutorial adds delete behavior. The service still owns the , the component still owns temporary UI state, and the managed collection still flows through the same pipeline. The new part is the delete write path: the service now submits a selected identity through mergeState() while keeping Feature ownership in the same place.

Focus on the boundary: keep deletion policy in the service, keep confirmation state in the component, and route the removal through a normal Feature update instead of an ad hoc mutable array operation. To do that, add a removeCharacter() method that submits the target identity through mergeState() with isDelete: true, and keep the confirmation flow in a local delete-candidate Signal. The important constraint does not change: the component coordinates the destructive action, but it still does not mutate committed Feature State directly.

Make the Change
  1. Open example.service.ts and add a removeCharacter() method. @for (file of serviceFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
  2. Add the withArrayMergeId to the initialization chain. 
    {{ 
                  `this.#vault?.withArrayMergeId?.({ idKey: 'id' }).initialize();` 
                  }}
  3. The updateCharacter() uses mergeState() so Array By ID Merge replaces the matching character by identifier.
  4. Keep the service as the only place that calls the destructive update API.
  5. Submit the target identity with isDelete: true so unknown IDs leave the visible State equivalent.
What to Look For
  • Delete remains a service-owned write path just like add and edit.
  • mergeState() with isDelete: true is the right operation for removal because Array By ID Merge applies the identity-based rule.
  • The removal rule is identity-based, so one matching record is removed while every other record is preserved.
  • The component will request deletion, but the service still owns the mutation and supplies the delete configuration.
Step 3: Update the Component and HTML for Delete
↑ top

The delete tutorial is complete once the page can stage a pending delete, cancel that destructive action, confirm removal of the selected record, and react cleanly when the collection becomes smaller or empty. The boundary still has not moved: the service owns the , and the component owns only local selection, editor, confirmation, and feedback state.

This chapter keeps the implementation disciplined even while it adds a destructive action. The component presents a confirmation panel, clears local selection after a confirmed removal, and returns the editor to a safe create-ready state. The architectural rule stays fixed: the component does not call APIs directly, and it does not own committed Feature State. Delete is routed through the same service-owned boundary as every other mutation.

Unknown or Stale IDs

removeCharacter() submits the target identity through mergeState() with isDelete: true. When the ID is absent, Array By ID Merge leaves the collection equivalent; the example does not treat that as an error or create a record. The service spec verifies the resulting value, not an emission-count guarantee. In a multi-writer application, revalidate the pending record at confirmation time. Any success feedback shown for a stale ID is a tutorial limitation, not an authoritative server acknowledgment; report the stale deletion instead of claiming success.

Delete Outcome Contract
Action FeatureCell request Expected result
Cancel delete No request Clears only the component's delete candidate. The collection and selection remain unchanged.
Confirm a known ID mergeState() with isDelete: true Removes the matching record, clears selection and the form, and returns the editor to create mode. Every nonmatching record is retained.
Confirm a stale ID mergeState() with isDelete: true Leaves the collection equivalent. This tutorial makes no promise about subscriber emission for equivalent array values.
What to Look For
  • Cancel preserves the record; confirm removes only that identity and clears stale local selection.
  • The component coordinates confirmation while the service owns the identifier-based merge request.
  • Save this checkpoint for Chapter 5 and reload it after testing terminal destruction.
Step 4: Chapter Round-up
↑ top

The Delete Characters chapter is complete once characters can be deleted successfully.

Run and Verify
  1. Select Leia Organa and note the five-record count. Cancel deletion and confirm the count remains five and Leia remains selected.
  2. Request deletion again, confirm it, and verify that the count becomes four, Leia disappears, selection clears, and Luke Skywalker remains unchanged. The empty-state guidance appears after the last record is removed.
Chapter 5 Summary
  • The component now owns a delete-confirmation state in addition to its existing selection and editor state.
  • The template adds an explicit destructive-action checkpoint instead of deleting immediately from the current selection.
  • The service now supports full create, update, and delete operations through the same boundary.
